before.content_html:
What Is Musical Form?

In music, form (also called structure) refers to how a piece of music is organised into sections. Composers use form to give their music shape and to help listeners follow what is happening. In the Eduqas GCSE Music exam (AoS1), you need to identify and describe common musical forms when listening to extracts. Two of the most important forms you must know are binary form and ternary form.

To label sections in music, we use letters of the alphabet. Each new letter represents a section that sounds different — it has contrasting musical material. When a letter is repeated, it means that section returns, either exactly as before or with some variation.

Binary Form (AB)

Binary form is one of the simplest musical structures. A piece in binary form has two distinct sections, labelled A and B. Each section usually sounds different from the other, meaning there is contrast between them.

Here are the key features of binary form:

  • Two sections: Section A presents an opening musical idea. Section B introduces contrasting material — this might be a different melody, a change of key, a shift in dynamics, or a new rhythmic pattern.
  • No return of A: Unlike ternary form, the A section does not come back at the end. Once section B begins, the piece continues in that new direction until it finishes.
  • Repeat marks: In many Baroque and Classical pieces, both sections are repeated, giving a structure of AA BB (or written with repeat marks as ||: A :||: B :||). Even with repeats, the overall form is still binary.
  • Key changes: In tonal music, section A often begins in the tonic key and modulates (changes key) towards the end — commonly to the dominant (in major keys) or the relative major (in minor keys). Section B often begins in this new key and works its way back to the tonic by the end.
Key Fact

Binary form = AB. Two contrasting sections with no return of the opening material. Think of it as a musical journey that goes somewhere new and stays there.

Binary form was very popular in Baroque dance music (around 1600–1750). Dances such as the minuet, bourrée, gavotte, and gigue were commonly written in binary form. Many of J.S. Bach’s keyboard suites contain movements in binary form. You will also find binary form in some folk songs and hymns where verse 1 uses one melody and verse 2 uses a different one, with neither returning.

Ternary Form (ABA)

Ternary form has three sections, labelled A B A. The first section (A) presents the main musical idea. The middle section (B) provides contrast. Then the A section returns at the end, creating a sense of balance and completeness.

Here are the key features of ternary form:

  • Three sections: Section A is the opening idea. Section B is a contrasting middle section. Section A then returns — either exactly the same or slightly varied.
  • Contrast in B: The middle section typically contrasts with A through changes in melody, key, tempo, dynamics, texture, or mood. A common approach is for A to be in a major key and B to shift to the relative minor (or vice versa).
  • Return of A: This is the defining feature that separates ternary from binary. The return of A gives the listener a feeling of coming home. If the final section sounds the same as the opening, you are hearing ternary form.
  • Da capo: In some scores, the return of A is indicated by the instruction da capo (Italian for “from the beginning”), which tells the performer to go back to the start. This is why ternary form is sometimes called da capo form.
Key Fact

Ternary form = ABA. The return of the A section at the end is what makes it different from binary form. If A comes back, it’s ternary. If it doesn’t, it’s binary.

Ternary form is found across many genres and periods. Classical minuets with a trio section follow a ternary plan (Minuet – Trio – Minuet). Many Romantic piano pieces, such as Chopin’s nocturnes, use ternary form. Pop songs that follow a verse–bridge–verse pattern can also be described as ternary. In the Eduqas composition briefs, students are sometimes asked to compose in ternary form — for example, composing a piece for an evening concert in ternary form for piano plus one other instrument.

Comparing Binary and Ternary Form

The table below summarises the key differences. Being able to quickly spot these differences in a listening exam is essential.

Binary form (AB): Two sections. No return of A. Contrast between A and B. Often uses repeat marks. Common in Baroque dances.

Ternary form (ABA): Three sections. A returns at the end. Contrast in middle B section. Often uses da capo. Common in Classical minuets and Romantic character pieces.

Shared features: Both use contrasting sections. Both can feature key changes. Both are found across many musical periods and styles.

How to Identify These Forms in the Listening Exam

When you hear an extract in the exam, follow these steps to work out the form:

  • Step 1 — Listen for sections: Does the music clearly change at any point? A new melody, key, or mood signals a new section.
  • Step 2 — Count the sections: Can you hear two distinct parts (AB) or three (ABA)?
  • Step 3 — Listen for the return: Does the opening material come back after the contrasting section? If yes, it is ternary. If the music simply moves on and ends without returning, it is binary.
  • Step 4 — Check for repeats: Don’t be tricked by repeat marks. If both sections are repeated (AABB), it is still binary form — the A section is only being repeated immediately, not returning after B.
Key Fact

The single most important question to ask yourself: “Does the opening section come back after the contrasting section?” If yes → ternary (ABA). If no → binary (AB).

Contrast Between Sections

Whether you are listening or composing, you need to understand how contrast is created between sections. Composers use a combination of the following musical elements to make their B section sound different from A:

  • Melody: A new melodic idea or theme is introduced.
  • Key / Tonality: The music modulates to a related key (e.g. from C major to G major, or from A minor to C major).
  • Dynamics: A loud A section might contrast with a quiet B section, or vice versa.
  • Tempo: The speed may change — though this is less common in binary and ternary form than in other structures.
  • Texture: The number of parts or layers of sound may change. For example, section A might be homophonic while section B becomes thinner or thicker.
  • Rhythm: Different rhythmic patterns or note values may be used.

If your Eduqas composition brief asks you to write in ternary form, you must clearly show three sections: A, B, and A (returning). Your B section should contrast with A — try changing the key, using a new melody, or altering the dynamics and texture. When A returns, you can bring it back exactly or add slight variations (e.g. extra ornamentation, a fuller texture, or a slightly different ending). Make sure your structure is clear enough for the listener to hear.

Minuet and Trio

The minuet and trio is a special case of ternary form that you are very likely to encounter in the exam. It originated as a stately dance in the Classical era (c.1750–1820), always written in 3/4 time at a moderate tempo.

The structure follows a clear ABA pattern:

  • Minuet (A): The opening dance section, often with an elegant, graceful character. Internally, the Minuet itself is frequently in binary form (two repeated sections), though it functions as the “A” of the larger ternary structure.
  • Trio (B): A contrasting middle section, usually in a different but related key. The Trio typically has a lighter texture, fewer instruments, and a gentler character. The name “trio” comes from an older convention where this section was played by three instruments.
  • Minuet da capo (A): The Minuet returns exactly as before. In the score, this is often indicated by the instruction da capo (“from the beginning”) rather than writing the music out again.

This form is a textbook example of ternary (ABA), where A is the Minuet and B is the Trio. Haydn and Mozart used the minuet and trio as the third movement in many of their symphonies and string quartets. Beethoven later replaced it with the faster scherzo and trio, but the ternary structure remained identical.

Key Fact

To identify a minuet and trio in the exam, look for these features together: (1) 3/4 time signature with a moderate, dance-like character, (2) a contrasting Trio section that is lighter in texture or in a different key, and (3) a da capo return of the opening Minuet. If the music has an ABA structure but is not in 3/4 or lacks the dance character, it is more likely plain ternary form.

If you hear an ABA piece in the exam, ask yourself two questions: “Is it in 3/4 time?” and “Does it have a dance-like, elegant feel?” If both answers are yes and you notice a lighter contrasting middle section, call it a minuet and trio — this is more specific than just saying “ternary form” and will earn more marks. Typical features to mention include balanced phrases (often 4 or 8 bars long), a homophonic texture, and clear contrasts in key and instrumentation between the Minuet and Trio sections.
before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas listening exam, if you are asked to identify the form of a piece, write the letter labels clearly — “binary form (AB)” or “ternary form (ABA)”. If the question asks you to describe the structure, don’t just name it. Go further: explain how the sections contrast (e.g. “Section B introduces a new melody in the relative minor”) and whether the return of A is exact or varied. Use specific musical vocabulary such as “modulation”, “contrast”, and “da capo” to pick up extra marks. A common mistake is confusing binary form with repeated sections — remember, AABB is still binary because A does not return after B.

Possible answers: • Introducing a new or different melody in section B. • Modulating to a different key (e.g. from the tonic to the dominant or relative minor). • Changing the dynamics (e.g. from forte to piano). • Changing the texture (e.g. from homophonic to thinner/polyphonic). • Using different rhythmic patterns. • Changing the tempo.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between binary form and ternary form. Refer to the structure and use of sections in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks: 4 marks. Possible answers: • Binary form has two sections (AB) while ternary form has three sections (ABA) (1 mark). • In binary form, the A section does not return after B (1 mark). • In ternary form, the A section returns after B, creating a sense of balance or completeness (1 mark). • Both forms use contrast between sections, but ternary has the added feature of recapping the opening material (1 mark). • Credit use of correct terminology such as modulation, da capo, tonic, dominant (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: A piece of music begins with a lively melody in D major. A contrasting section follows in B minor with a different melody and quieter dynamics. The opening melody then returns in D major. Explain what form this piece is in and how you can tell. Use musical vocabulary in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
practice_questions.marks: 6 marks across two levels. Upper band (4-6): Clearly identifies ternary form (ABA). Explains that the opening section returns after the contrasting middle section. Uses correct vocabulary (e.g. modulation, tonic, contrast, da capo). Identifies specific contrasting features: change of key from D major to B minor, quieter dynamics, different melody. Explains that the return of A creates balance. Lower band (1-3): Identifies ternary form but gives limited explanation. May describe some contrast but without precise vocabulary. May not clearly explain why the return of A is significant.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the similarities and differences between binary form and ternary form. In your answer, refer to the structure, use of contrast, and how each form is used in different styles of music.
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
practice_questions.marks: 8 marks (QWC assessed). Top band (7-8): Thorough and detailed discussion. Clearly defines both forms (AB and ABA). Explains how contrast is created between sections in both forms (key, melody, dynamics, texture, rhythm). Explains the key difference — the return of A in ternary form. Gives examples of where each form is used (e.g. binary in Baroque dances, ternary in Classical minuets, Romantic piano pieces, or pop music). Uses accurate musical terminology throughout. Well-organised writing with clear communication. Upper-mid band (5-6): Good discussion with mostly accurate detail. Defines both forms correctly. Describes some methods of contrast. Mentions at least one example or context for each form. Mostly accurate terminology. Lower-mid band (3-4): Some relevant points but lacks detail or accuracy. May confuse some features. Limited use of examples or terminology. Lower band (1-2): Basic awareness of the forms. May only describe one form or give vague or inaccurate information.

before.content_html:
Rondo Form

Rondo form is a structure built around one idea: a catchy main theme that keeps coming back. The main theme is labelled ‘A’, and each time it returns it is separated by contrasting sections called episodes. The most common pattern is ABACA, but longer rondos can extend to ABACADA or even further.

Think of the A section as a musical “home base.” No matter how far the music travels into new episodes, it always returns to A. This gives rondo form a strong sense of unity, while the contrasting episodes provide variety and keep the listener interested.

Key Fact

The structure of rondo form is ABACA (or longer). The ‘A’ section is the recurring main theme. The ‘B’ and ‘C’ sections are contrasting episodes. In your exam, if you hear the same theme returning between different sections, it is very likely rondo form.

How Rondo Creates Contrast

The episodes (B, C, etc.) contrast with the main theme in several ways. Composers might change the key, use a different melody, alter the texture, or shift the dynamics. For example, if the A section is in a major key with a lively melody, the B section might move to the relative minor with a smoother, more lyrical idea.

Each time the A section returns, it is usually heard in the home key (the tonic). This return gives the listener a satisfying sense of familiarity. The A section may be repeated exactly, or the composer may add small changes such as ornamentation or a different accompaniment to keep it fresh.

Mozart’s Eine Kleine Nachtmusik (Third Movement) is a well-known example of rondo form from the Classical era (c.1750–1820). The A section features balanced phrases and a homophonic texture with the violins carrying the melody. Each episode introduces contrasting material before the familiar A theme returns. The Classical style favours clear, balanced melodies and regular phrasing, which makes rondo form easy to follow.

Theme and Variation Form

Theme and variation form takes a different approach to creating contrast. Instead of alternating between a theme and separate episodes, the composer presents one theme and then transforms it through a series of variations. The structure is labelled A, A1, A2, A3 and so on, where each number represents a new variation.

The original theme is usually simple and memorable — this makes it easier for the listener to recognise how it changes. Each variation keeps something from the original (often the harmonic structure or the basic shape of the melody) while altering other elements.

Key Fact

Theme and variation form is structured as A, A1, A2, A3, etc. Each variation is based on the original theme but changes elements such as melody, rhythm, tempo, dynamics, texture, key, or ornamentation. The theme should always be recognisable underneath the changes.

What Can Change in a Variation?

Composers have many tools available to vary a theme. Here are the most common techniques you need to know for your exam:

Melody: The tune may be decorated with ornamentation (trills, mordents, turns), or the rhythm of the melody might be altered while keeping the same pitches.

Rhythm and tempo: The note values may change — for example, the theme could be played in quicker notes (diminution) or slower notes (augmentation). The tempo might shift from fast to slow or vice versa.

Harmony and key: A variation might switch from major to minor (or minor to major), or use more complex chords. Chromaticism might be introduced in Romantic-era variations.

Texture: The accompaniment might change from block chords to broken chords (like an Alberti bass), or the texture could shift from homophonic to contrapuntal.

Dynamics: A loud, bold theme could become quiet and delicate, or gradual crescendos and diminuendos could be added.

Instrumentation: In orchestral works, different instruments might take over the melody in each variation, changing the timbre of the music.

Theme and Variation Across the Eras

Theme and variation form was popular across all three eras of the Western Classical Tradition (1650–1910). In the Baroque era (c.1600–1750), variations might feature terraced dynamics, ornamentation, and a basso continuo. In the Classical era (c.1750–1820), composers like Haydn used balanced phrases and clear harmonic changes. Haydn’s “Surprise” Symphony No. 94 in G Major (2nd Movement) is a famous example of theme and variations. In the Romantic era (c.1820–1900), composers introduced more dramatic changes including rubato, wider dynamic ranges, and chromaticism.

Rondo uses a main theme (A) that returns between completely different episodes (B, C, etc.). The episodes are new, separate ideas. The structure creates contrast by alternating between familiar and unfamiliar material.

Theme and variation keeps the same underlying theme throughout but transforms it each time. There are no separate episodes — every section is based on the original theme. The contrast comes from how the theme is changed, not from introducing entirely new material.

In your exam, ask yourself: “Am I hearing the same theme come back unchanged between different sections?” If yes, it is likely rondo. “Am I hearing the same theme but with changes each time?” If yes, it is likely theme and variation.

Recognising These Forms in the Exam

In the Eduqas GCSE listening exam, AoS1 questions will test your ability to identify and describe musical forms. Here are some practical tips for spotting rondo and theme and variation:

Rondo clues: Listen for a distinctive theme that returns at least twice. Between each return, you should hear clearly different music. The main theme usually returns in the tonic key. You may hear the label ABACA in a question — this confirms rondo form.

Theme and variation clues: Listen for a theme at the start, then notice how subsequent sections sound similar but altered. You might hear the same chord progression or melodic shape, but the rhythm, speed, dynamics, or instruments will change. If every section relates back to the opening theme, it is likely theme and variation (A, A1, A2, A3).

Key Fact

In the exam, you may be asked to underline or identify the correct structure. Remember: Rondo = ABACA (recurring theme with contrasting episodes). Theme and Variation = A, A1, A2, A3 (same theme, modified each time). Always listen for whether contrasting sections are new ideas (rondo) or transformations of the original theme (theme and variation).

Strophic Form

Strophic form is one of the simplest structures in music. The same music is repeated for every verse, but with different words each time. The structure is labelled A–A–A–A (and so on for however many verses there are).

Strophic form is extremely common in:

  • Hymns and carols — the congregation sings the same tune for each verse with different words.
  • Folk songs — traditional songs often tell a story across several verses, all set to the same melody.
  • Simple pop songs — some pop songs repeat the same musical section for each verse without a contrasting chorus.

A well-known classical example is Schubert’s Heidenröslein, where the same graceful melody is sung three times with different words telling the story of a boy and a rose.

Key Fact

Strophic form = same tune, new words each time (A–A–A–A). The melody stays the same across every verse. It is common in hymns, folk songs, and carols.

The opposite of strophic form is through-composed form. In a through-composed piece, the music changes with each verse — no section is repeated. The composer writes new music for every part of the text. Schubert’s Erlkönig is a famous through-composed song: the music constantly evolves to reflect the dramatic story of a father riding through the night with his dying child.

In the exam, if you hear the melody repeating exactly while the words change, it is strophic. If the music keeps changing and nothing comes back, it is through-composed. Most real music falls somewhere in between, but these two terms represent the extremes.

before.description: Learn the six key musical devices: sequence, ostinato, imitation, pedal, drone, and canon.
before.content_html:
What Are Musical Devices?

Musical devices are techniques that composers use to develop, decorate, and add interest to their music. In the Eduqas GCSE Music specification for AoS1, you need to know six key devices: sequence, ostinato, imitation, pedal, drone, and canon. These devices appear across Baroque, Classical, and Romantic music — the whole span of the Western Classical Tradition (1650–1910) that AoS1 covers.

Being able to identify these devices by ear and describe how they are used is essential for the listening exam. You should also consider using them in your own compositions, as the free composition briefs for AoS1 specifically ask you to “make use of sequence” and other devices.

Sequence

A sequence is when a musical pattern — usually a short melodic phrase — is immediately repeated at a higher or lower pitch. If the pattern moves up in pitch each time, it is called an ascending sequence. If it moves down, it is a descending sequence.

Sequences are very common in Baroque music. In Vivaldi’s Winter from The Four Seasons, the solo violin uses ascending sequences during the second section to portray “biting, stinging winds.” The motif is heard three times, each time at a higher pitch, creating a sense of rising intensity. Sequences help composers extend a short idea into a longer passage without introducing completely new material.

Key Fact

A sequence repeats a melodic or rhythmic pattern at a different pitch level. Listen for the same shape of notes stepping up or stepping down. In the exam, state whether the sequence is ascending or descending and give a bar number if you can.

Ostinato

An ostinato is a short musical pattern — melodic, rhythmic, or both — that repeats continuously throughout a section or an entire piece. It acts like an anchor, giving the music a strong sense of pulse and unity while other parts change above or around it.

A famous example is the introduction to Toto’s Africa, where “Riff b” (bars 3–4) uses an ostinato pattern of five notes based on the E major pentatonic scale over a sustained chord ii (C♯m). The ostinato groupings cut across the 2/2 time signature, creating syncopation rooted in African musical traditions. In the Baroque period, an ostinato bass line (sometimes called a ground bass) was a common feature, with a repeating bass pattern supporting changing harmonies and melodies above.

In popular music, a repeated pattern is often called a riff. In classical and exam contexts, the correct term is ostinato. They describe a very similar idea — a short, catchy pattern that loops — but “ostinato” is the term the exam expects. A riff might only appear in certain sections (like a guitar riff in the chorus), whereas a true ostinato tends to repeat persistently throughout a section or the whole piece.

Imitation

Imitation is when a musical idea is heard in one part and then copied closely — but not exactly — by another part a short time later. Think of it as one instrument “echoing” what another has just played. The copy usually enters before the first part has finished, so the two parts overlap.

Imitation is a key feature of contrapuntal texture, which was especially important in the Baroque era (c.1600–1750). Composers like Bach used imitation extensively in fugues, where a subject is introduced in one voice and then imitated by other voices entering one by one. In the listening exam, if you hear a melody appear in one instrument and then a similar version starting shortly after in a different instrument, you are likely hearing imitation.

Pedal

A pedal (also called a pedal note or pedal point) is a note that is sustained or continuously repeated, usually in the bass, while the harmonies and melodies above it change freely. The most common pedal notes are the tonic pedal (based on the home note of the key) and the dominant pedal (based on the fifth note of the key).

In Vivaldi’s Winter, a tonic pedal appears in the opening section as the orchestral strings create a cold, still atmosphere. The held bass note grounds the harmony while the upper parts create gentle dissonance above it. A dominant pedal is often used to build tension before a final cadence, because it creates anticipation that the music will resolve back to the tonic.

Key Fact

A pedal note is usually in the bass, but it can also appear in the highest part — this is called an inverted pedal. In the exam, always state which type of pedal you hear (tonic or dominant) and where it is (bass or upper part).

Drone

A drone is one or more sustained notes that sound continuously beneath a melody. Unlike a pedal, which is typically a single note in the bass that underpins changing harmony, a drone usually involves two notes (often the tonic and the dominant) and tends to last for very long stretches of music — sometimes an entire piece.

Drones are commonly associated with folk music traditions, such as the sound of bagpipes, where a continuous low note hums while the melody is played on top. In Western classical music, drones appear at the beginnings and endings of pieces to establish the key firmly. Think of a drone as a constant, unchanging sound bed that gives the music a sense of stability or even monotony.

Students often confuse pedal and drone because both involve sustained notes. Here is a simple way to tell them apart. A pedal is a single sustained or repeated note (usually tonic or dominant) in the bass, and the harmonies above it change — sometimes clashing with the pedal note. A drone usually involves two sustained notes (tonic and dominant together) and typically lasts much longer — sometimes the whole piece. If the held note is short-lived and the harmony moves around it, call it a pedal. If it is continuous and unchanging throughout, call it a drone.

Canon

A canon is a device where two or more parts play exactly the same melody but start at different times, so they overlap. The most well-known example is Frère Jacques — when sung as a round, each voice enters with the same tune a few bars apart. That is a canon.

In classical music, Pachelbel’s Canon in D is the most famous example. Three violin parts play the same melody, each entering a few bars after the previous one, over a repeating bass line (an ostinato). Canon creates a rich, layered texture because multiple versions of the melody sound simultaneously. It is closely related to imitation, but the key difference is that in a canon the melody is copied exactly, whereas in imitation the copy may be altered slightly.

Both canon and imitation involve one part copying another, but they are not the same thing. In a canon, the second part copies the melody exactly — note for note, rhythm for rhythm. In imitation, the second part copies the idea closely but not identically — it may change some notes, intervals, or rhythms. If the exam asks you to identify which device is being used, listen carefully: is the copy exact or approximate?

Repetition and Contrast

Repetition is the most fundamental compositional tool in music. When a composer restates a musical idea — whether it is a melody, a rhythm, or a chord pattern — the listener recognises it and feels a sense of unity and familiarity. Without repetition, music would sound random and impossible to follow.

Contrast is the opposite: introducing something new and different. This might be a change of key, texture, dynamics, rhythm, or melodic character. Contrast creates variety and keeps the listener’s attention.

The two devices work hand in hand. Too much repetition and the music becomes boring. Too much contrast and the music sounds incoherent — like a series of unrelated ideas. Every well-crafted piece of music balances repetition and contrast. In binary form (AB), section A is stated and section B provides contrast. In ternary form (ABA), the return of A uses repetition to frame the contrasting B section.

Key Fact

Repetition creates unity and familiarity. Contrast creates variety and interest. Together, they form the backbone of every musical structure. In the exam, you can describe how a composer uses repetition to unify a piece and contrast to keep it engaging.

Broken Chord, Arpeggio and Alberti Bass

A broken chord is created when the notes of a chord are played separately rather than all at once. Instead of striking all three (or four) notes together, the performer plays them one at a time. This creates a flowing, rippling effect often used in accompaniments.

An arpeggio is a specific type of broken chord where the notes are played in order — from the bottom note to the top (or top to bottom). Think of it as running up or down the notes of a chord like a ladder.

The Alberti bass is a very specific broken chord pattern that was hugely popular in Classical-era keyboard music. Named after the Italian composer Domenico Alberti (c.1710–1740), it plays the notes of a chord in the pattern: bottom – top – middle – top. For example, if the chord is C major (C–E–G), the Alberti bass plays C–G–E–G, C–G–E–G, over and over in the left hand.

Mozart and Haydn used the Alberti bass constantly in their piano sonatas. It provides a gentle, flowing harmonic accompaniment beneath a singing melody in the right hand. If you hear a rippling left-hand pattern in a Classical keyboard piece, it is very likely an Alberti bass.

Key Fact

Broken chord = notes of a chord played separately. Arpeggio = broken chord played in order (low to high or high to low). Alberti bass = a specific pattern of bottom–top–middle–top, common in Mozart and Haydn piano music. In the exam, listen for a repeating left-hand pattern beneath a melody — if it follows the bottom–top–middle–top shape, call it an Alberti bass.

Regular Phrasing and Motifs

Regular phrasing means the melody is organised into balanced phrases of equal length — most commonly 4-bar or 8-bar phrases. These phrases often come in pairs known as antecedent and consequent (or question and answer). The first phrase ends on an unfinished-sounding chord (like the dominant), and the second phrase responds by finishing on the tonic — giving a sense of completion.

Regular phrasing is characteristic of Classical-era music (Mozart, Haydn, Beethoven) and gives the music a sense of order and elegance.

A melodic motif is a short, memorable melodic idea — sometimes just two or three notes — that forms the building block of a composition. A rhythmic motif is a short rhythmic pattern that serves the same function. Motifs are the DNA of a composition: composers repeat them, vary them, put them in sequence, invert them (turn them upside down), and combine them in new ways to build an entire piece from a tiny seed.

Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 is the classic example: the famous four-note motif (short–short–short–long) drives the entire first movement, appearing in different keys, dynamics, and instruments throughout.

Key Fact

Regular phrasing = balanced 4-bar or 8-bar phrases, often in question-and-answer pairs. A motif is a short musical idea (melodic or rhythmic) used as a building block. Composers develop motifs through repetition, sequence, inversion, variation, and augmentation/diminution. In the exam, if a short idea keeps reappearing in different forms, call it a motif.

Several other musical devices appear across this unit. Here is where to find them:

  • Anacrusis, Syncopation, Dotted rhythms → Musical Elements Lesson 2 (Dynamics, Tempo and Rhythm)
  • Conjunct/Disjunct movement, Ornamentation → Musical Elements Lesson 1 (Melody and Articulation)
  • Chord progressions, Modulation, Cadences → Musical Elements Lesson 4 (Harmony and Tonality)

How These Devices Appear Across the Eras

The six devices are not limited to one era. However, some are more closely associated with particular periods:

Baroque (c.1600–1750)

Imitation, Sequence, Pedal, Canon, Ostinato

Contrapuntal texture was central to Baroque music, so imitation and canon were extremely common. Composers like Bach and Vivaldi used sequences to develop melodic ideas, pedal notes (especially tonic pedals) to anchor harmonies, and ground bass ostinatos to unify whole movements.

Classical (c.1750–1820)

Sequence, Pedal

Classical composers like Mozart and Haydn favoured homophonic texture and balanced phrases, but they still used sequences to extend melodic ideas and dominant pedals to build tension before cadences. Imitation appears less frequently but is still present in development sections.

Romantic (c.1820–1900)

Pedal, Ostinato, Sequence

Romantic composers used pedal notes and ostinatos to create dramatic tension and sustain emotional moods. Sequences were used alongside chromaticism to build intensity. Drones appear in pieces influenced by folk music traditions.

Spotting Devices in the Listening Exam

In the Eduqas listening exam, you may be asked to identify a device by name, give a bar number where it occurs, or explain how a device is used to create a particular effect. Here is a quick checklist for each device:

Key Fact

Quick identification guide: Sequence — same pattern, different pitch. Ostinato — short pattern repeating over and over. Imitation — one part echoes another closely but not exactly. Pedal — one held or repeated bass note while harmonies change. Drone — continuous sustained notes (often two) throughout. Canon — exact copy of a melody starting at a different time.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six AoS1 musical devices are sequence, ostinato, imitation, pedal, drone, and canon — know the definition and sound of each.
  • Canon uses an exact copy of a melody at a different starting time; imitation uses a close but not identical copy.
  • Always specify the type of pedal (tonic or dominant) and distinguish between a pedal (single note, shorter duration) and a drone (often two notes, sustained throughout).

practice_questions.text: Name the musical device where a melodic pattern is repeated at a higher or lower pitch.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark(s) for: Sequence.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between a pedal and a drone.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per valid difference, up to 2 marks. Possible answers:
• A pedal is usually a single sustained/repeated note; a drone often involves two notes (tonic and dominant) (1).
• A pedal is typically shorter in duration and occurs within a section; a drone tends to last much longer, sometimes throughout an entire piece (1).
• A pedal usually has changing harmonies above it that may create dissonance; a drone provides a constant, unchanging sound bed (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how an ostinato is used in a piece of music you have studied.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks for a clear description. Possible answers (e.g. referencing Africa by Toto or a Baroque ground bass):
• An ostinato is a short repeating pattern (1).
• In Toto's Africa, Riff b uses a five-note ostinato based on the pentatonic scale (1).
• It repeats over a sustained chord (C#m) in the introduction (1).
• The irregular groupings create syncopation that cuts across the 2/2 time signature (1).
Credit any valid studied example with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between imitation and canon. Give an example of each in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• In imitation, a musical idea is heard in one part and then copied closely but not exactly by another part (1).
• In canon, the melody is copied exactly, note for note (1).
• Valid example of imitation, e.g. fugues by Bach where the subject is altered slightly in subsequent entries (1).
• Valid example of canon, e.g. Pachelbel's Canon in D where three violin parts play the same melody entering at different times (1).

practice_questions.text: Give a bar number during the extract where one example of the following musical features occurs: an ascending sequence.
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark(s) for a correct bar number where an ascending sequence occurs in the given extract. Accept any bar number that accurately shows a melodic pattern repeated at a higher pitch. (This question is modelled on the Eduqas prepared extract format.)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the following musical devices are used in music from the Western Classical Tradition (1650–1910): sequence, pedal, and ostinato. In your answer, refer to their musical effect and give examples from specific eras where possible.
practice_questions.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (7-10): Thorough, detailed response covering all three devices with accurate musical vocabulary. Clear examples from specific eras. Explains the effect of each device convincingly.
Mid band (4-6): Sound understanding of at least two devices. Some use of musical vocabulary. At least one era-specific example. Some explanation of effect.
Lower band (1-3): Basic understanding of one or two devices. Limited musical vocabulary. Vague or no examples.
0 marks: No valid content.
Indicative content:
• Sequence: a melodic pattern repeated at a higher or lower pitch; used in Baroque music (e.g. Vivaldi) to extend ideas and build intensity; ascending sequences create excitement, descending sequences can create a sense of falling or sadness.
• Pedal: a sustained or repeated bass note (tonic or dominant) while harmonies change above; common in Baroque (e.g. tonic pedal in Vivaldi's Winter creates stillness); dominant pedals build tension before cadences in Classical and Romantic music.
• Ostinato: a short repeating pattern; Baroque ground bass is a type of ostinato; creates unity and drives the music forward; also appears in Romantic music to sustain mood.

practice_questions.text: Identify the time signature used throughout the Badinerie.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark(s) for: 2/4 (simple duple).

practice_questions.text: Give a bar number where one example of each of the following musical features occurs: (i) a natural sign, (ii) a slur mark, (iii) a demisemiquaver.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each correct bar number (3 marks total). Accept any valid bar number where the feature is present in the score. For a natural sign, accept e.g. bar 16, 17, 18. For a slur mark, accept any bar where a slur appears in any part. For a demisemiquaver, accept e.g. bar 33 or bar 34.

practice_questions.text: The extract begins in F# minor. Other than B minor, name two keys to which the music modulates during Section B.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each correct key (2 marks total). Accept: E minor (1 mark) and D major (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two musical features of the Badinerie which are typical of Baroque music.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks: 1 marks for each valid Baroque feature described (max 2 marks). Accept any two from: • Use of basso continuo / harpsichord and cello providing continuo • Terraced dynamics (sudden shifts in volume rather than gradual) • Use of ornaments such as trills and appoggiaturas • Binary form structure • Use of sequences as a compositional device • Diatonic harmony with perfect and imperfect cadences • Transverse flute as a solo instrument • Figured bass notation. Must describe the feature, not just name it, for full credit.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Bach develops motif X throughout the Badinerie. Refer to specific bars in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
practice_questions.marks: Answers may include: • Motif X first appears in bars 0²–2¹ in the flute as a descending B minor arpeggio (1 mark) • In bars 6²–8¹ it is given to the cellos with a modified ending (quaver + 2 semiquavers) and begins a sequence moving to A major (1 mark) • In bars 8²–10¹ the cello continues with further modification (4 semiquavers), completing the sequence in F# minor (1 mark) • In bars 18²–20¹ the motif is inverted (ascending) and divided between two instruments, moving to E minor (1 mark) • In bars 28²–32¹ the cello sequence from Section A returns transposed (1 mark) • In bars 32²–34¹ motif X becomes a conversation between flute and 1st violin, decorated with an appoggiatura and demisemiquavers (1 mark) • In bars 36²–38¹ motif X is inverted and divided between instruments again (1 mark) • In bars 38²–40¹ the cellos close Section B with an altered pitch shape and less active rhythm (1 mark). Award marks for accurate references to specific bars and clear description of how the motif is changed.

practice_questions.text: This piece was composed during the Baroque era. Discuss how the Badinerie demonstrates typical features of Baroque music in its melody, harmony, texture, and use of instruments. In your answer you must refer to specific musical details from the piece.
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (9-12): Detailed and perceptive response covering most musical elements with accurate bar references. Mid band (5-8): Sound response covering several elements with some specific references. Lower band (1-4): Limited response with few specific references.
Content may include:
• Melody: Based on two motifs (X and Y); motif X is a descending broken chord; motif Y is ascending semiquavers. Ornaments include trills (bars 8, 10, 15, 27, 30, 32) and appoggiaturas (bars 33, 40). Sequences used in bars 6²–10¹ and 28²–32¹. Inversion of motif X in bars 18²–20¹.
• Harmony: Diatonic throughout. Modulates to related keys (F# minor, E minor, D major). Perfect and imperfect cadences. Chords in inversion. V7 in third inversion. Neapolitan sixth chord in bar 35. Suspensions in bars 8¹, 10¹, 32¹.
• Texture: Homophonic (melody and accompaniment). Flute carries main melody; cello provides bass line and melodic material; 2nd violin and viola provide harmony.
• Instruments: Transverse flute, string orchestra, harpsichord (basso continuo). Figured bass used. Typical Baroque ensemble.
• Other: Binary form (AABB). Terraced dynamics. 2/4 time. Allegro tempo. Simple ostinato rhythms.

before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas listening exam, the Badinerie appears as a prepared extract with score worth 12 marks. You will be given the score and hear the extract three times. Practise reading the score before the exam so you can quickly locate bar numbers. Common question types include: identifying musical features at specific bar numbers (e.g. natural signs, slurs, demisemiquavers), naming chords marked with asterisks, identifying cadence types, naming keys the music modulates to, and describing Baroque features. Always give specific bar numbers in your answers where possible — vague answers lose marks. If asked to describe Baroque features, link them directly to the piece (e.g. “terraced dynamics are used, with sudden shifts in volume rather than gradual crescendos”).
before.content_html:
Background: Bach and the Badinerie

Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and musician of the Baroque era. He was born on 31st March 1685 and died on 28th July 1750. Bach is known for instrumental works such as the Brandenburg Concertos and the Goldberg Variations, and vocal music such as the St Matthew Passion and the Mass in B minor. He is generally regarded as one of the greatest composers of all time.

The Badinerie is the final movement of Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 2 in B minor, composed in 1738–1739. The suite contains seven movements: Overture, Rondeau, Sarabande, Bourrée, Polonaise, Menuet and Badinerie. A suite is a collection of short pieces, usually dances, played one after another. The word “badinerie” means something playful or teasing, and the music reflects this with its fast tempo and lively flute part.

Key Fact

The Badinerie is scored for transverse flute, string orchestra (Violin 1, Violin 2, Viola, Cello) and harpsichord (basso continuo). The transverse flute is held horizontally, unlike a recorder which is held vertically. Basso continuo is a system of partially improvised accompaniment played above a bass line, typically by a keyboard instrument with the cello reinforcing the bass.

Form and Structure

The Badinerie is in binary form (AB), with each section repeated once to give AABB. This is a standard structure for Baroque dance movements.

Section A

Bars 02 – 161 (16 bars)

Begins in B minor (the tonic key) and ends in F# minor (the dominant minor). Both repeat marks are present, so the whole section is played twice.

Section B

Bars 162 – 401 (24 bars)

Begins in F# minor and modulates through E minor and D major (the relative major) before returning to the tonic key, B minor. Section B is longer than Section A and is also repeated.

Notice how Section A moves away from the tonic (B minor → F# minor), while Section B mirrors this by moving back to the tonic (F# minor → B minor). This tonal journey is a hallmark of binary form in the Baroque era.

Melody: Motifs X and Y

The entire movement is built on just two short musical ideas, called motif X and motif Y. Bach develops, modifies and passes these motifs between instruments throughout the piece.

Motif X is heard at the very start (bars 02–21) in the flute. It is a descending B minor arpeggio/broken chord with a characteristic quaver-and-semiquaver rhythm. This motif appears many times throughout the piece in modified forms:

Bars 62–81: Motif X moves to the cellos in a modified version — the final crotchet is replaced with a quaver and two semiquavers. This shifts the tonality to A major and begins a sequence.

Bars 82–101: Motif X continues in the cellos with its ending further modified (four semiquavers). It moves the tonality to F# minor and completes the answering phrase of the sequence.

Bars 182–201 (Section B): Motif X is inverted so that it ascends rather than descends. It is also divided between two instruments. This moves the tonality to E minor.

Bars 322–341: Motif X becomes part of a musical conversation between the flute and the 1st violin. It is decorated by an appoggiatura and rapid demisemiquaver movement.

Motif Y first appears in bars 22–41 in the flute. It is an ascending semiquaver figure consisting of arpeggios/broken chords and conjunct (stepwise) movement.

Bars 102–121: Motif Y returns in the flute with a modified ending — the last two quavers are replaced by four semiquavers.

Bars 122–161: Motif Y is extended and developed (labelled Y1 in the analysis). Section A closes in F# minor.

Bars 222–241 (Section B): Motif Y returns with the same modified ending as bars 102–121, but transposed into a new key.

Bars 342–361: Motif Y returns with a modified beginning — the first four semiquavers are replaced by a quaver and four demisemiquavers.

Harmony and Tonality

The harmony is diatonic throughout. The piece begins in B minor and modulates to closely related keys. The key scheme is carefully structured:

Section A: B minor → A major → F# minor (dominant minor). Section B: F# minor → E minor → D major (relative major) → B minor (tonic). Both perfect cadences and imperfect cadences appear clearly throughout the movement.

Key Fact

Chords frequently occur in inversion, with occasional use of V7 in third inversion. A Neapolitan sixth chord appears in bar 35. Suspensions occur in bars 81, 101 and 321.

Rhythm, Metre and Tempo

The time signature is 2/4 (simple duple) throughout. The tempo is Allegro (fast), though this is not marked on the original score — this was typical of the Baroque period. The rhythms are built from simple ostinato patterns using almost entirely quavers and semiquavers, with occasional demisemiquavers used as decoration (e.g. bars 32–34).

Texture and Instrumentation

The texture is homophonic (melody and accompaniment). The flute carries the main melody for most of the movement. The cello provides important melodic material too, especially during the sequences in bars 62–101 and 282–321. The 1st violin joins in occasionally (e.g. the musical conversation in bars 322–341), while the 2nd violin and viola provide harmony with less busy lines.

The dynamics are mostly forte, with terraced dynamics (sudden shifts between loud and quiet rather than gradual crescendos and diminuendos). Very few dynamic markings appear on the score, which was typical of the period.

Baroque Features in the Badinerie

The Badinerie is a perfect example of Baroque style. Here is a summary of the Baroque features you need to know for the exam:

Trills: Found in bars 81, 101, 152, 272, 301 and 321.

Appoggiaturas: Found in bars 331 and 401.

Sequences: Found in bars 62–101 and bars 282–321. A sequence is the repetition of a motif at a higher or lower pitch.

Inversion: In bars 182–201 and 362–381, motif X is inverted so it ascends rather than descends.

Basso continuo: The harpsichord and cello provide continuous accompaniment, with the harpsichord reading from figured bass.

Terraced dynamics: Volume shifts suddenly rather than gradually.

Diatonic harmony: The harmony stays within closely related keys.

Binary form: A standard structure for Baroque dance movements.

Instrumentation: Use of transverse flute, strings and harpsichord is typical of a Baroque orchestral suite.

Key Fact

The flute part has a two-octave pitch range. The entire movement is built from just two motifs (X and Y) which are constantly modified, extended, inverted and passed between instruments. This motivic development is a key feature of Bach’s compositional style.
